entry.evidence: the aim of the research of this paper is to present the anomalies of air pressure registered after the passage of the shock wave

sequences.source_document: Published paper (publisher XML text, PDF for figures)

steps.action: Cite the Krakatoa 1883 barograph records as precedent that an eruption shock wave produces pressure anomalies around the globe.
steps.quote: the shock wave, visible through pressure anomalies on barographs, traveled the planet Earth at least four times

steps.action: Take eruption facts (plume heights, timing, energy) from Tonga services, the Smithsonian and NASA, and the global 2-3 hPa pressure jump reported by Díaz and Rigby.
steps.quote: a jump of 2–3 hPa, which was registered at all meteorological stations on Earth

steps.action: Pose the aim: present the pressure anomalies recorded in Serbia during passage of the HT–HH shock wave.
steps.quote: present the anomalies of air pressure registered after the passage of the shock wave

steps.action: State the working hypothesis: treating the atmosphere as a fluid, a link to the eruption must appear as pressure peaks at Serbian stations.
steps.quote: then this connection must be manifested in the form of anomalies (peaks) of air pressure on the MS in Serbia

steps.action: Obtain pressure records of the live event from 4 automatic stations of the Serbian service at different sites and altitudes, plus Podgorica barograph data.
steps.quote: [...] pressure were obtained from the Republic Hydrometeorological Service of Serbia, from 4 MS

steps.action: Use spherical trigonometry to derive the Belgrade–volcano great-circle distance (16,952.65 km), the antipode in Algeria, and the expected arrival directions of the first and second waves.
steps.quote: the shock wave moved radially from the point T2 to the antipodal point T2ʹ along the orthodrome

steps.action: Define speed equations (distance over time elapsed since the 04:00 UTC eruption) for each wave arrival and their average, and make azimuthal maps with the NS6T tool.
steps.quote: For the purposes of this research, the speed of the shock wave propagation was also calculated

steps.action: Name the rival: cyclonic or anticyclonic weather systems, not the eruption, could have caused the pressure peaks.
steps.quote: it was necessary to remove the suspicion that the occurrence of pressure peaks was caused by the existing synoptic situation

steps.action: Read the 500 hPa and surface pressure maps for 15 January 00–18 UTC and 16 January 00 UTC, which show a stable anticyclone over Serbia.
steps.quote: both on the surface and in the upper-level, a stable atmosphere can be seen above Serbia and the Balkan Peninsula

steps.action: Check the synoptic reading against SYNOP-based analytical maps and NMME-DREAM model pressure fields for 18 UTC and 00 UTC.
steps.quote: In order to verify the above, analytical maps, which were made on the basis of SYNOP reports from MS across Europe, were also analyzed.

steps.action: Exclude the synoptic rival as a cause of the sudden pressure jumps.
steps.quote: the synoptic situation could not cause fluctuations in air pressure on the MS included in the analysis

steps.action: Reason from fluid behaviour that pressure waves spread globally; show the southward first wave and northward second wave on azimuthal maps.
steps.quote: pressure waves will appear on the entire Earth as a consequence

steps.action: Read the station pressure graphs: first peak about 19 UTC on 15 January, second about 00 UTC on 16 January, each followed by 2-3 h of oscillation.
steps.quote: The first peak of air pressure (increase in air pressure by 1.5 hPa/h) was registered on January 15 at around 19:00 UTC.

steps.action: Match the first and second peaks to the expected southward and northward wave arrivals.
steps.quote: [...] of air pressure is the consequence of the southward-propagating part of the shock wave.

steps.action: Identify a third peak at Stara Planina around 08 UTC on 17 January as the first wave's return after circling the Earth.
steps.quote: On January 17, most likely around 08:00 UTC, the first pressure wave return was registered on the Stara Planina MS

steps.action: Verify the peaks at an independent station, Podgorica (Montenegro), using its SYNOP pressure-tendency groups 52012 and 52008.
steps.quote: In order to verify the previous statement, an analysis of the SYNOP report of the main MS Podgorica (Montenegro) was performed.

steps.action: Compute wave speeds from distance and elapsed time: 1,130 km/h (first wave), 1,000.75 km/h (second), 1,095 km/h (return), average 1,079.8 km/h.
steps.quote: Using Eqs. (3), (4), (5), and (6), the approximate speed of the first shock wave of 1,130 km h–1 was obtained.

steps.action: Compare the speeds with the speed of sound, the Bureau of Meteorology of Australia's reported speeds above 1,000 km/h, and media reports of audibility in Alaska.
steps.quote: the confirmation of this claim is the statement of the Bureau of Meteorology of Australia

steps.action: Keep the claim that the pressure changes in Serbia and Montenegro were caused by the HT–HH eruption, with the derived timings and speeds.
steps.quote: after proving that the changes in air pressure in Serbia (and Montenegro) are a consequence of the HT–HH eruption.

steps.action: Extend the result to a general statement that any atmospheric disturbance affects the global atmosphere, without a further test.
steps.quote: any disturbance in the Earth's atmosphere, regardless of geographical location, has an impact on the global atmosphere

end.claim: Pressure anomalies at Serbian (and Montenegrin) stations around 19 UTC on 15 January, 00 UTC on 16 January and 08 UTC on 17 January 2022 were shock-wave arrivals from the HT–HH eruption, not synoptic effects, travelling at about 1,130 km/h.

decisive_move.sentence: Reading the pressure records of the four Serbian stations, which show peaks at the expected arrival times in a stable atmosphere, is what the attribution and speed estimate rest on.

gates.evidence: Action: the hypothesis (§1.1 ¶1) guided which records were pulled, but the data were routine station records collected regardless. Claim: the synoptic rival could have explained the peaks and was checked (§2.1), but arrival times were not predicted before the records were read and no failure criterion was stated. Registration: nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Assumption that the atmosphere behaves as a fluid, so disturbances propagate globally
Cosine formula for an oblique spherical triangle, antipode calculation, Postel and azimuthal projections
Alaska Public Media and Weather Channel reports of audibility and wave circuits

limits: No uncertainty is given on arrival times or speeds. Arrivals are read as 'around' a given hour, and t0 is set to 04:00 UTC (footnote 7, p. 6), so the speed sub-claim is an estimate without stated resolution (estimate_with_resolution, weak). Inference: the second-wave speed (1,000.75 km/h) equals 20,015 km over 20 h, which conflicts with the z1 = 3,062 km of Eq. 2; the paper does not explain which distance it used. The return wave (best_explanation) rests on one station (Stara Planina). The 'same meridians' generalization rests on one extra station (Podgorica). The rival exclusion is qualitative, from synoptic charts; no filtering, detrending or background-noise statistics are reported. The Fig. 7 time axes are in CET and the UTC conversion is done by the reader. The closing generalization (any disturbance affects the global atmosphere) is not tested. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown. Entry coded as anomaly; 'hypothesis' is a defensible alternative, since the paper calls its fluid assumption the 'initial hypothesis' (§1.1 ¶1), but that hypothesis was framed after the event.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Time origin t0 = first stronger eruption at 04:00 UTC on 15 January
alternatives_considered.alternatives: None named explicitly; earlier eruptive activity on 13–14 January is described in §1 ¶5
